Fixed in ca64d2327.

I considered the suggested "always run isBlockedAddress()" but that would re-block the entire RFC1918/CGNAT space and make the flag a no-op — the whole point of `allowPrivateNetworkHooks` is to reach first-party VPC-internal endpoints. So I went with a layered approach instead:

- `ssrfGuard.ts` gains `METADATA_IPS` (`169.254.169.254`, `100.100.100.200`) and `isMetadataAddress()`, which normalizes IPv4-mapped IPv6 forms (`::ffff:a9fe:a9fe`, `::ffff:169.254.169.254`, `0:0:0:0:0:ffff:a9fe:a9fe`, ...) through the existing `extractMappedIPv4`/`expandIPv6Groups` helpers.
- `isBlocked()` now runs the metadata check unconditionally for IP literals; only the general range check (`isBlockedAddress`) is skipped when the flag is on.

`http://[::ffff:a9fe:a9fe]/latest/meta-data` is now blocked with the flag on (tests added in `urlValidator.test.ts` and `httpHookRunner.test.ts`).

**[Critical]** When `allowPrivateNetworkHosts` is true, this early return skips DNS resolution entirely. The only SSRF protection upstream is `UrlValidator.isBlocked()`, which checks the URL hostname string against `BLOCKED_HOSTS` — but this only catches **literal** metadata hostnames like `169.254.169.254`. Any hostname that DNS-resolves to a cloud metadata IP passes unchecked because the resolved IP is never inspected. — Failure scenario: an admin enables `allowPrivateNetworkHooks` for VPC-internal hooks. A hook URL `http://internal-gateway.example.com/hook` where DNS resolves to `169.254.169.254` passes `isBlocked()` (not a literal metadata hostname, not an IP literal) and `validateResolvedHost` returns `{ok: true}` without DNS resolution. `fetch()` connects to the cloud metadata endpoint, exposing IAM tokens and SSH keys.

Suggested fix: when the flag is on, still perform DNS resolution and check resolved IPs against known cloud metadata addresses (at minimum `169.254.169.254` and `100.100.100.200`), rather than skipping the entire function.

_— qwen3.7-max via Qwen Code /review_

Fixed in ca64d2327. The early return is gone: with the flag on, `validateResolvedHost` still resolves the hostname via `dns.lookup(all: true)` and checks every resolved address — but now only against `isMetadataAddress()` (169.254.169.254 / 100.100.100.200, including IPv4-mapped forms) instead of the full range check. A hostname resolving to a metadata IP is blocked even with the flag on; DNS resolution failure still defers to fetch as before. Tests added for both metadata IPs under the flag-on path.

Fixed in ca64d2327. `100.100.100.200` is now in the new `METADATA_IPS` set in `ssrfGuard.ts` and is matched by `isMetadataAddress()` in all serialized forms (plain IPv4, `::ffff:6464:64c8`, `::ffff:100.100.100.200`) — unconditionally, regardless of the flag, both at the URL layer and after DNS resolution. `http://100.100.100.200/latest/meta-data` is blocked with the flag on (tests added).

Confirmed and fixed in 26f7c99. You are right that the scan reads a literal argument as a redirection — and the consequence is worse than the split alone. At the previous head:

```
"echo a \> & rm -rf /"  => ["echo a \> & rm -rf /"]
   ops ["write_file:/repo/rm"]
```

The `rm -rf /` was not merely joined to the previous segment, it was invisible as a command — `extractShellOperations` read the `\>` as a redirect and reported a *write to `/repo/rm`* instead. Now:

```
"echo a \> & rm -rf /"  => ["echo a \>", "rm -rf /"]
   ops ["edit:/"]
```

The scan now counts the backslashes before the `>`/`<` it lands on and treats an odd count as an escape:

```ts
if (ch === ">" || ch === "<") {
  // Escaped, so a literal argument and the `&` still backgrounds.
  return precedingBackslashCount(command, j) % 2 === 1;
}
```

Tests added for both `\>` and `\<`, plus an over-correction guard that `echo a \\>& 2` (escaped *backslash*, so a real descriptor duplication) still does not split.

**[Critical]** Adding `&` as a segment boundary makes `walkCompoundCommand` (in `shell-semantics.ts`) apply foreground-`cd` cwd semantics to a *backgrounded* `cd`, which in bash does not change the parent shell's cwd. Failure scenario: `cd /tmp & echo {} > settings.json` in `/repo` — bash backgrounds `cd /tmp` (parent cwd stays `/repo`), but `walkCompoundCommand` shifts `effectiveCwd` to `/tmp` and attributes the redirect write to `/tmp/settings.json`. A deny/ask rule protecting `/repo/settings.json` never matches. Suggested fix: propagate the boundary operator from `splitCompoundCommand` to `walkCompoundCommand`; for a `cd` segment separated by `&`, do not shift `effectiveCwd`.

Verified this against the code and it's real: `isManagedDirectoryName` (`skill-curator.ts:253`) only checked the `auto-skill-` prefix and `path.basename === name`, and `displayName` in `curator-command.ts:50-53` concatenates `entry.directoryName` verbatim into the lines the non-interactive `/curator` path writes to stdout — which, unlike the TUI (`HistoryItemDisplay.tsx` `escapeAnsiCtrlCodes`), has no ANSI guard. A crafted `auto-skill-<ESC>…` directory with a valid `SKILL.md` reaches that output, so the injection is reachable.

Fixed by requiring the directory name to match the skill-name charset, but with one correction to the suggested patch: the suggested regex `/^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]+$/` is ASCII-only, whereas `SKILL_NAME_PATTERN` (`types.js:262`) is `/^[\p{L}\p{N}_:.-]+$/u` — Unicode-aware. Since a managed directory is always `auto-skill-<name>` where `<name>` passes `validateSkillName` and the prefix chars are within that same set, gating on `SKILL_NAME_PATTERN` never rejects a legitimately generated directory (including non-ASCII skill names, which the ASCII-only guard would silently drop from the curator), while still excluding ESC/control bytes — `\x1b` is neither `\p{L}`, `\p{N}`, nor the allowed punctuation.

Added a regression test (`ignores auto-skill directories whose names carry control/ANSI bytes`) that seeds a crafted directory carrying a *valid* frontmatter `name`, so only the directory-name guard can exclude it — the test fails if the charset check regresses. All 19 curator tests pass; typecheck and lint clean. Pushed in 171ac3fc.

Verified against the code and fixed. `readManagedSkill` did read the manifest inside `Promise.all([lstat(dir), lstat(manifest), readFile(manifest)])`, so `readFile` followed a symlinked `SKILL.md` concurrently with — not after — the `isSymbolicLink()` guard, letting a `/dev/zero` target begin an unbounded read before the guard's `undefined` return took effect.

Now `lstat`s the directory first, then reads the manifest through a shared `readRegularFileNoFollow` helper that opens with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK` and `fstat`s the descriptor: a symlink is refused atomically at open (ELOOP), a FIFO/non-regular file is rejected by the fstat guard, and the read is bounded by `MAX_MANIFEST_BYTES` (4 MiB, well above any real manifest) via the same fd it reads. This matches the existing `O_NOFOLLOW` convention in `gitUtils.ts`/`gitDiff.ts`. Added a regression test (`refuses an auto-skill whose manifest is a symlink`). Curator + rollback tests, typecheck, and eslint are green. Pushed in 4915a72.

discussion_comments.comment_body:
**[Suggestion]** The scan range `[^;&|\n]*?` does not stop at `--` (end-of-options separator) or redirect operators (`>`, `<`), so `-f` or `--force` on the far side of those operators is matched as if it were a flag when bash tokenizes it as a pathspec or redirect target.

Failure scenario: `git clean -d -- -f` (clean targeting a file literally named `-f`) or `git clean > -f` (redirect stdout to a file named `-f`) are both flagged as destructive. Without the actual force flag, `git clean` deletes nothing in either case. The old regex (`/\bgit\s+clean\s+-[a-zA-Z]*f/`) required the flag immediately after `git clean\s+` and did not have this false positive.

Practical impact is low (files named `-f` are rare, and `git clean` without `-f` would error anyway), but the scan crosses operator boundaries that bash itself respects.

```suggestion
  /\bgit\s+clean\b(?:(?!--)[^;&|<>\n])*?(?:\s-[a-zA-Z]*f|\s--force\b)/,
```

_— qwen3.7-max via Qwen Code /review_

discussion_comments.comment_body:
The false positives are real and they are mine — the old regex anchored the flag to `git clean\s+` so it never crossed a `--`, and widening the scan is what let it. I ran both in a scratch repo to confirm they are no-ops: `git clean -d -- -f` and `git clean > -f` both exit 128 with `fatal: clean.requireForce is true and -f not given: refusing to clean`, untracked count unchanged (bash does create a file named `-f` for the redirect form, as you say).

But I can't take the suggested pattern, because `(?!--)` stops the scan at *every* `--`, not just the end-of-options one — and `--quiet`, `--exclude=` and `--force` all start with `--`. `--force` survives only because the lazy quantifier tries the alternation before consuming; any other long option in front of the flag ends the scan. Excluding `>` costs the redirect forms separately. I ran each of these in a scratch repo and counted untracked entries before/after:

| command | current | suggested | actually does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `git clean --quiet -fd` | BLOCK | **allow** | deletes everything (4 → 0) |
| `git clean --exclude=build -f` | BLOCK | **allow** | deletes (4 → 3) |
| `git clean -d --exclude=dist --force` | BLOCK | **allow** | deletes (4 → 1) |
| `git clean 2>/dev/null -fd` | BLOCK | **allow** | deletes everything (4 → 0) |
| `git clean -d -- -f` | **BLOCK** | allow | nothing — git refuses |
| `git clean > -f` | **BLOCK** | allow | nothing — git refuses |
| `git clean -fd` / `-d -f` / `-d --force` / `--force -d` | BLOCK | BLOCK | deletes |
| `git clean -d 'my dir' -f` / `-d $(pwd) -f` | BLOCK | BLOCK | deletes |
| `git clean -n` / `-nd` / `; tail -f log` / `&& grep -f pat f` | allow | allow | — |

Net: it removes 3 prompts on commands git refuses to run and adds 4 silent executions of commands that really do delete untracked files. `git clean --quiet -fd` and `git clean -d --exclude=dist --force` are not exotic spellings; those are how you'd write it in a script.

The `--` half is fixable without that cost, by stopping at a *standalone* `--` token rather than at any `--`:

```
/\bgit\s+clean\b(?:(?!\s--(?:\s|$))[^;&|\n])*?(?:\s-[a-zA-Z]*f|\s--force\b)/
```

That keeps all 13 destructive cases above and drops 2 of the 3 false positives, leaving only `git clean > -f` — which can't be closed without excluding `>` and losing `2>/dev/null -fd` with it. Its own cost is a `--` appearing inside a quoted argument ahead of the flag (`git clean -e 'a -- b' -f`), which fails open.

So it's one contrived false positive against one contrived false negative, and I'd rather keep the guard erring toward the prompt: the current cost is a confirmation dialog on a command that does nothing, and the alternative cost is untracked files deleted with no prompt at all. Happy to apply it if you'd rather have the tighter match — say the word and I'll push it with tests for all six new vectors.

总体来看：它消除了 3 次对 git 本来就拒绝执行的命令的确认提示，却新增了 4 条真正会删除未跟踪文件、且无任何提示的命令。`git clean --quiet -fd` 和 `git clean -d --exclude=dist --force` 并不是什么冷僻写法，脚本里就是这么写的。

`--` 这一半可以在不付出上述代价的前提下修复——只在*独立的* `--` 记号处停止，而不是在任意 `--` 处停止：

```
/\bgit\s+clean\b(?:(?!\s--(?:\s|$))[^;&|\n])*?(?:\s-[a-zA-Z]*f|\s--force\b)/
```

它保留了上表全部 13 条破坏性命令，并消除了 3 个误报中的 2 个，只剩下 `git clean > -f`——而这一个若不排除 `>` 就无法解决，排除后又会连带丢失 `2>/dev/null -fd`。它自身的代价是标志前的引号参数中出现 `--`（如 `git clean -e 'a -- b' -f`），这属于失效放行。

所以这是一个牵强的误报对一个牵强的漏报，我更倾向于让这道防线偏向提示：当前的代价是对一条什么都不做的命令弹出确认框，而另一种的代价是未跟踪文件被静默删除、完全没有提示。如果你更希望匹配更精确，我很乐意采用——说一声，我就连同这 6 个新用例的测试一起提交。
